population: Adults at rest (educational demo). Not validated for children, pregnancy, athletes, or people with known conditions.
disclaimer: These rules are simplified, educational thresholds drawn from public general-audience guidance. They are not a diagnostic tool, have not been clinically validated in this software, and must not be used for medical decisions.

rules.explanation: The reading is above the commonly cited adult resting range of 60–100 bpm. Exercise, caffeine, stress, fever, or a measurement taken while active can all raise heart rate.
rules.source: American Heart Association — 'All About Heart Rate (Pulse)': normal adult resting heart rate 60–100 bpm.
rules.limitations: Only meaningful for resting measurements. Does not consider activity, medication, or individual baselines.

rules.message: Resting heart rate well above 100 bpm
rules.explanation: The reading is far above the commonly cited adult resting range of 60–100 bpm. The 130 bpm escalation level is a project-chosen demonstration threshold.
rules.source: Base range: American Heart Association (60–100 bpm). 130 bpm escalation level: project-chosen demonstration threshold.
rules.limitations: Escalation level is not a clinical standard. Exercise readings will trigger it.

rules.explanation: The reading is below the commonly cited adult resting range. Well-trained athletes and people during sleep often have lower heart rates without any problem.
rules.source: American Heart Association — normal adult resting heart rate 60–100 bpm; 50 bpm used here to reduce false alarms (project choice).
rules.limitations: Frequently normal for athletes. Does not consider medication (e.g. beta-blockers).

rules.explanation: The reading is far below the commonly cited adult resting range. The 40 bpm level is a project-chosen demonstration threshold.
rules.source: Project-chosen demonstration threshold relative to AHA 60–100 bpm range.
rules.limitations: Not a clinical standard. Device or entry errors are common at extreme values.

rules.explanation: Typical pulse-oximeter readings for healthy adults are 95–100%. Cold fingers, nail polish, movement, and skin pigmentation can affect accuracy.
rules.source: NHS — 'How to use a pulse oximeter at home': readings of 93–94% warrant seeking advice; typical healthy range 95–100%.
rules.limitations: Consumer pulse oximeters have known accuracy limits, including reduced accuracy on darker skin tones (FDA safety communication, 2021).

rules.explanation: Public guidance treats 92% or lower on a home pulse oximeter as a level that needs urgent attention.
rules.source: NHS — 'How to use a pulse oximeter at home': 92% or below needs urgent attention.
rules.limitations: Some people with chronic lung conditions have different personal targets set by their clinicians.

rules.explanation: A temperature of 38.0 °C (100.4 °F) or higher is the common public-health definition of a fever.
rules.source: CDC — fever defined as a measured temperature of 100.4 °F (38 °C) or greater.
rules.limitations: Measurement site (oral, ear, forehead) changes readings by up to ~0.5 °C.

rules.explanation: General public guidance suggests adults contact a health professional for a temperature of 103 °F (39.4 °C) or higher.
rules.source: Mayo Clinic — 'Fever: First aid': adults should call a provider at 103 °F (39.4 °C) or higher.
rules.limitations: Does not consider symptoms, duration, or age-specific guidance.

rules.explanation: A body temperature below 35 °C (95 °F) is the common definition of hypothermia. Low readings are also often caused by measurement error.
rules.source: CDC / Mayo Clinic — hypothermia defined as body temperature below 95 °F (35 °C).
rules.limitations: Forehead and ear thermometers frequently under-read in cold environments.

rules.message: Blood pressure in the Stage 1 range (systolic 130–139 or diastolic 80–89 mmHg)
rules.explanation: This range is labelled 'Stage 1' in the ACC/AHA blood pressure categories. A single reading is not enough to categorize anyone; categories are based on repeated measurements.
rules.source: 2017 ACC/AHA Guideline for High Blood Pressure in Adults — blood pressure categories.
rules.limitations: Single home readings vary with posture, cuff size, and recent activity.

rules.message: Blood pressure at or above 140/90 mmHg
rules.explanation: This range is labelled 'Stage 2' in the ACC/AHA blood pressure categories. Repeated readings in this range are worth discussing with a health professional.
rules.source: 2017 ACC/AHA Guideline for High Blood Pressure in Adults — blood pressure categories.
rules.limitations: Single home readings vary; white-coat and masked effects exist.

rules.explanation: The American Heart Association describes readings above 180/120 mmHg as a 'hypertensive crisis' level and advises re-measuring and seeking care, especially if symptoms are present.
rules.source: American Heart Association — 'Understanding Blood Pressure Readings' (hypertensive crisis > 180 and/or > 120).
rules.limitations: Re-measurement after resting is recommended before interpreting a single value.

rules.explanation: Readings below 90/60 mmHg are commonly described as low blood pressure. Many people have naturally low blood pressure without symptoms.
rules.source: American Heart Association / NHS — low blood pressure commonly described as below 90/60 mmHg.
rules.limitations: Often normal for some individuals; symptoms matter more than the number alone.

rules.explanation: Public-health guidance recommends at least 7 hours of sleep per night for adults.
rules.source: CDC / American Academy of Sleep Medicine — adults 18–60 should sleep 7 or more hours per night.
rules.limitations: Self-reported or tracker-estimated sleep is approximate.

rules.explanation: Well below the recommended 7+ hours for adults. The 5-hour level is a project-chosen demonstration threshold.
rules.source: Base recommendation: CDC / AASM (7+ hours). 5-hour level: project-chosen demonstration threshold.
rules.limitations: Escalation level is not a clinical standard.

trend_rules.message: Weight changed by 2 kg or more within 7 days
trend_rules.explanation: A noticeable short-term weight change. Hydration, clothing, scale differences, and time of day commonly cause swings of 1–2 kg.
trend_rules.source: Project-chosen demonstration threshold (general advice that unexplained rapid weight change is worth discussing with a professional).
trend_rules.limitations: Not a clinical standard; does not distinguish intended from unintended change.
